claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a homogeneous, high-temperature single-phase BCC structure.
Phase instability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is driven by differential elemental diffusion during cooling or subsequent thermal exposure.
Slow cooling or extended thermal exposure enables Cr and Al to partition locally within the BCC matrix.
Local Cr and Al partitioning promotes atomic-scale chemical ordering.
Atomic-scale ordering nucleates secondary phases such as B2 or sigma within the BCC matrix.
Al has faster atomic mobility than Cr in this alloy.
The difference between Al and Cr diffusivities produces local enrichment zones during slow cooling.
Chemical ordering in the enrichment zones lowers free energy through formation of ordered structures.
Formation of ordered secondary structures embedded in the BCC matrix destabilizes the single-phase state.
Slow cooling or prolonged annealing permits more atomic redistribution than rapid quenching.
Rapid quenching suppresses redistribution and retains a uniform single-phase BCC structure with minimal ordering.
Relative to rapidly quenched specimens, slow-cooled or annealed specimens will show additional diffraction peaks from secondary ordered phases.
Relative to rapidly quenched specimens, slow-cooled or annealed specimens will contain observable precipitates and phase boundaries.
The precipitated or segregated regions will be enriched in both Cr and Al.
The diffusion-driven phase change may alter mechanical properties.
The mechanism should not operate when cooling is too rapid for significant elemental redistribution.
The identity and volume fraction of the secondary phase are not specified and may involve B2, sigma, or another phase.

An absence of new diffraction peaks, precipitates, and chemical segregation after slow cooling or annealing relative to the quenched baseline would falsify the proposed differential-diffusion mechanism.

contradictions.description: The stated initial condition is a solid high-temperature BCC phase, but the baseline is described as quenching directly from the melt. Quenching a liquid and quenching from within the solid BCC stability field are different starting conditions and do not define a strictly controlled comparison.
